clinicalPearls: Bartonella are fastidious, facultative intracellular, slow-growing gram-negative bacteria; clinical presentation depends on both the infecting species and the host's immune status. Of the >40 species/subspecies, B. bacilliformis, B. quintana and B. henselae are most commonly identified human pathogens (p.1350).

B. henselae is the principal etiologic agent of cat-scratch disease (CSD); rare cases are associated with Afipia felis and other Bartonella species. Apparently healthy bacteremic cats (especially kittens) are the major reservoir; person-to-person transmission does not occur and intrafamilial clustering is rare (p.1351).

Typical CSD (85-90% of cases) is a usually self-limited subacute regional lymphadenopathy; a small (0.3-1 cm) painless erythematous papule/pustule appears at the inoculation site within days to 2 weeks in about one-third to two-thirds of patients, with nodes enlarging 1-3 weeks (or longer) after cat contact (p.1351-1352).

Affected nodes are usually painful and suppurate in ~10% of cases; axillary/epitrochlear nodes are most commonly involved, then head/neck, then inguinal/femoral. About 50% have fever, malaise and anorexia; weight loss and night sweats can mimic lymphoma (p.1351-1352).

Atypical (extranodal) CSD occurs in 10-15% and includes Parinaud's oculoglandular syndrome, neuroretinitis (often unilateral visual deterioration), hepatosplenic disease, encephalitis/seizures/myelitis/cranial-nerve palsies, FUO, pneumonitis, debilitating myalgia, arthritis/arthralgia (mostly women >20 yr), osteomyelitis (incl. multifocal) and erythema nodosum (p.1353).

CSD-associated FUO is a unique, sometimes severe and debilitating syndrome that often mimics malignancy and may involve multiple organs (hepatosplenic space-occupying lesions, abdominal/mediastinal lymphadenopathy, ocular disease, multifocal osteomyelitis); fever may be continuous or relapsing (p.1353).
In elderly patients (>60 yr), lymphadenopathy is more often absent, whereas encephalitis and FUO are more common than in younger patients (p.1353).

Coxiella burnetii and Bartonella species are the most common causes of culture-negative endocarditis; in one French series Bartonella accounted for 28% of 348 culture-negative endocarditis cases. B. quintana and B. henselae are the species most often implicated (p.1353).

Bartonella endocarditis often presents as a prolonged, minimally febrile or even afebrile indolent illness lasting weeks to months; initial echocardiography may not show vegetations and acute aggressive disease is rare. Most cases are native-valve, ~60% aortic; B. henselae usually infects preexisting valvulopathy while B. quintana often infects normal valves (p.1353).

Bacillary angiomatosis (caused by B. henselae or B. quintana) is a neovascular proliferative disease of severely immunocompromised patients, presenting as non-painful tan/red/purple cutaneous lesions, tender subcutaneous nodules, ulcerated plaques or verrucous growths; nodular forms resemble fungal or mycobacterial infection (p.1354-1355).

Bacillary peliosis is a related angioproliferative disorder caused by B. henselae involving primarily the liver (peliosis hepatis) and also spleen and lymph nodes, with blood-filled cystic structures (microscopic to several mm). In advanced immunodeficiency, B. henselae and B. quintana are important causes of FUO (p.1355).

Trench fever (5-day/quintan fever) is caused by B. quintana, transmitted by the human body louse; it has reemerged as chronic bacteremia in homeless people (urban/contemporary trench fever), with alcoholism and louse infestation as risk factors (p.1354).
harrison.pathophysiology: Bartonella adapt to specific domestic/wild mammalian hosts where prolonged intraerythrocytic and endothelial-cell infection creates an immune-protected reservoir, producing chronic bacteremia that may persist even after prolonged antimicrobial therapy. Adhesion and entry to endothelial cells and erythrocytes is facilitated by Bartonella adhesin A or variably expressed outer-membrane proteins; the organism evades host immunity by modifying virulence factors (lipopolysaccharide, flagella) and attenuating the immune response. Humans are incidental hosts for most species except B. quintana and B. bacilliformis (which are not zoonotic). In CSD, the cat-to-human transmission mode is undetermined: B. henselae-infected cat saliva spreads to claws by self-licking and contaminated flea feces can be inoculated by a scratch or bite (mucous-membrane/conjunctival inoculation also possible). Lymphatic drainage to regional nodes in immunocompetent hosts triggers a TH1 response producing necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis, with dendritic cells and chemokines driving granuloma formation. In bacillary angiomatosis, Bartonella angiogenic factor A (a proangiogenic autotransporter in B. henselae) activates the host vascular endothelial growth factor pathway to drive angiogenesis (p.1350-1355).
nonInfectiousMimics: Lymphoma / malignancy (weight loss and night sweats of CSD, and CSD-associated FUO, can mimic malignancy)
Kaposi's sarcoma (differential for cutaneous bacillary angiomatosis)
Pyogenic granuloma (differential for cutaneous bacillary angiomatosis)
Subcutaneous tumors (differential for cutaneous bacillary angiomatosis)
additionalInvestigations: Serology (immunofluorescence or enzyme immunoassay) is the most commonly used diagnostic, but has variable sensitivity/specificity; CSD serodiagnosis is often based on IgG alone (in the absence of IgM) and seroconversion may take a few weeks, complicating interpretation (p.1352).

PCR of pus aspirated from a lymph node or the primary inoculation lesion is highly sensitive and specific and is particularly useful for definitive, rapid diagnosis in seronegative patients; PCR of a lymph node biopsy specimen may be less sensitive (possibly due to sampling error) (p.1352).

Histopathology shows early lymphoid hyperplasia, later stellate granulomata with necrosis, coalescing microabscesses and occasional multinucleated giant cells (nonspecific but may narrow the differential) (p.1352).

For endocarditis: blood cultures (even with lysis-centrifugation or EDTA tubes) are positive in only ~25% of cases (mostly B. quintana, rarely B. henselae) and require prolonged incubation up to 6 weeks; high-titer (>=1:800) IgG serology supports the diagnosis but cross-reacts between B. quintana and B. henselae and with C. burnetii and Chlamydia; species-level identification usually requires PCR and DNA sequencing of valve tissue (p.1353).

For bacillary angiomatosis/peliosis: diagnosis is by histologic examination; Warthin-Starry silver staining of lesions reveals clusters of bacilli; cultures are usually negative though blood cultures may be positive (p.1355).
redFlags: Persistent constitutional symptoms with failure of spontaneous regression of node size, and negative acute- and convalescent-phase sera (10-20% of CSD patients) — malignancy must be ruled out (p.1352).
Seronegative CSD with lymphadenopathy and severe complications (encephalitis or neuroretinitis) — early biopsy is important to establish a specific diagnosis (p.1352).
Unilateral visual deterioration (neuroretinitis) in suspected CSD — ophthalmologic manifestations may occasionally cause moderate to severe vision loss (p.1353).
Culture-negative endocarditis, especially in a homeless/alcoholic patient with body louse infestation (B. quintana) or significant cat exposure (B. henselae) (p.1353).
harrison.prognosis: In immunocompetent individuals, CSD (whether typical or atypical) usually resolves without treatment and without sequelae; resolution is slow, requiring weeks for fever/pain and months for node shrinkage, and lifelong immunity is the rule. Some ophthalmologic manifestations may occasionally result in moderate to severe vision loss. Bartonella endocarditis is often diagnosed late, and the proportion of patients requiring valvular surgery (~60%) is high, probably as a consequence of delayed diagnosis (p.1352-1353).
pitfalls: Bartonella is a key but easily missed cause of culture-negative endocarditis; routine blood cultures are positive in only ~25% of cases and serology cross-reacts with C. burnetii and Chlamydia, so a high titer to one organism may reflect cross-reactivity rather than the true pathogen (p.1353).
CSD is a frequently overlooked cause of FUO; CSD-associated FUO can mimic malignancy with multiorgan space-occupying lesions, leading to unnecessary investigation for cancer (p.1353).

Negative serology does not exclude CSD: 10-20% of patients have negative acute- and convalescent-phase sera, and seroconversion may take weeks; PCR of aspirated pus is preferred in seronegative patients (p.1352).
Suppurative nodes should be drained by large-bore needle aspiration, NOT by incision and drainage, to avoid chronic draining tracts (p.1353).
In elderly patients, lymphadenopathy is more often absent, so CSD may be missed when it presents instead as encephalitis or FUO (p.1353).
harrison.severityClassification: Cat-scratch disease is described along clinical lines rather than a formal grading scale: (1) Typical CSD (85-90%) — subacute regional lymphadenopathy, usually self-limited; (2) Atypical/extranodal CSD (10-15%) — extranodal manifestations (Parinaud's oculoglandular syndrome, neuroretinitis, hepatosplenic disease, neurologic disease, FUO, osteomyelitis, etc.). Severe/disseminated Bartonella disease (bacillary angiomatosis and peliosis) occurs primarily in HIV-infected persons with CD4+ T-cell counts <100/uL and in other immunosuppressed patients; Bartonella endocarditis is a separate severe culture-negative-endocarditis presentation (p.1351-1355).
